subject: physical-education
title: Movement Foundations and Safe Participation Routines
standards: Michigan PE Standard 1: Demonstrates competency in a variety of motor skills and movement patterns
Michigan PE Standard 2: Applies knowledge of concepts, principles, strategies and tactics related to movement and physical activities
Michigan PE Standard 4: Exhibits responsible personal and social behavior that respects self and others
essential_question: What routines keep people safe and ready to move well?
topics: self-space and general space under pressure
pathways, directions, and levels in combination
personal responsibility for the shared space

topic_content.name: self-space and general space under pressure
cues: Scan continuously; the space changes as others move.
Move into gaps rather than following the crowd.
Keep your head up even while controlling an object.
Anticipate where a gap will be, not where it is now.
topic_content.common_error: Watching only the nearest person. Fix: set tasks requiring learners to call out a far gap before travelling to it.

topic_content.name: speed, force, and controlled stopping
cues: Force is how hard you move; speed is how fast.
More speed needs more distance to stop safely.
Decelerate over several steps with a low, wide base.
Match force to the task — maximum is rarely correct.
topic_content.common_error: Full-speed running in a small space. Fix: shrink the area deliberately and require a controlled stop on signal.

topic_content.name: pathways, directions, and levels in combination
cues: Combine a pathway with a direction and a level for a richer movement.
Plan the combination before moving.
Changes should be visible to a watcher.
Repeat combinations to make them reliable.
topic_content.common_error: Combinations blur into a jog. Fix: require a watcher to name the pathway, direction, and level they saw.

topic_content.name: purposeful warm-up and cool-down design
cues: A warm-up should build gradually and prepare the specific joints you will use.
Match the warm-up to the activity that follows.
Cool-down lowers the heart rate progressively, then stretches.
Explain why each part is included.
topic_content.common_error: A generic warm-up unrelated to the session. Fix: require one movement in the warm-up that mirrors the main skill.

topic_content.name: equipment checks and safe setup
cues: Inspect equipment for damage, wear, and correct size.
Set up so nothing blocks a run-out or exit.
Leave space between stations.
Everyone knows the stop signal before starting.
topic_content.common_error: Stations placed too close, so run-outs overlap. Fix: walk the run-out of each station during setup.

topic_content.name: personal responsibility for the shared space
cues: Return equipment where it belongs.
Report damage rather than leaving it.
Look out for people around you, not just yourself.
Leave the area as safe as you found it.
topic_content.common_error: Leaving equipment out mid-session, creating trip hazards. Fix: assign a rotating equipment role each session.

performance_task: Design and lead a warm-up, area check, and cool-down for an adult or a group, justifying each element. A learner may instead write the plan and justify it.
adapted_alternative: Every travel task has a seated, supported, or reduced-range version: a learner may move through space in a wheelchair or walker, travel a shorter path, use arms only, or trace the pathway with a pointer or on paper. Speed is never the target; control is. Where a task mentions a group or a partner, a learner may work with one adult instead, or plan and justify it on paper, and that counts fully.

guardian_safety_review.equipment: Open floor space clear of furniture and trip hazards; non-slip footwear or bare feet on a safe surface.
guardian_safety_review.environment: Indoor open space, gym, or a cleared room. An outdoor lawn may be substituted.
guardian_safety_review.movement_hazards: Running and stopping in shared space. Guardian confirms the area is clear, the floor is not slippery, and boundaries are marked before the session.

subject: physical-education
title: Locomotor Combinations, Pathways, and Dynamic Space
standards: Michigan PE Standard 1: Demonstrates competency in a variety of motor skills and movement patterns
Michigan PE Standard 2: Applies knowledge of concepts, principles, strategies and tactics related to movement and physical activities
essential_question: How do I combine travel patterns and read space that keeps changing?
topics: changing direction and pathway at speed
chasing, fleeing, and dodging in shared space
reading and reacting to a moving partner

topic_content.name: combining locomotor patterns in sequence
cues: Transitions should be smooth, with no stumble or pause.
Change pattern on a count or a signal.
Vary level and pathway between patterns.
A repeatable sequence is a controlled one.
topic_content.common_error: Losing rhythm at the changeover. Fix: practise just the two-pattern join in isolation.

topic_content.name: travelling to open space
cues: Open space is where defenders and other players are not.
Move to space before you receive, not after.
Communicate that you are moving there.
Space closes quickly — commit once you decide.
topic_content.common_error: Standing still and calling for the object. Fix: require the learner to be moving as they call.

topic_content.name: changing direction and pathway at speed
cues: Lower your body slightly before cutting.
Push off the outside foot.
Make the change sharp and definite.
Accelerate out of the turn.
topic_content.common_error: Rounded turns that give away the intention. Fix: use cone gates that force a sharp angle.

topic_content.name: chasing, fleeing, and dodging in shared space
cues: When fleeing, use changes of direction and speed, not just straight running.
When chasing, watch the hips.
Fake one way and go the other.
Keep tags gentle and agreed.
topic_content.common_error: Fleeing in straight lines into corners. Fix: mark corner zones as out of play.

topic_content.name: jumping and landing with control
cues: Swing arms up on take-off.
Land on two feet where possible, toes then heels.
Bend knees and hips to absorb.
Land balanced and ready to move again.
topic_content.common_error: Landing on one stiff leg. Fix: require a held two-foot landing for three seconds before continuing.

topic_content.name: reading and reacting to a moving partner
cues: Watch the whole person, not just the object.
Mirror and match a partner movement to practise reacting.
React to what they do, rather than guessing early.
Stay balanced so you can move either way.
topic_content.common_error: Committing early and being beaten by a fake. Fix: play mirror games with no object so reading is the only task.

performance_task: Perform a travel sequence through a changing space and explain how you found and used open space.
adapted_alternative: Each locomotor pattern has an equivalent the learner can perform: arm-driven or wheelchair propulsion for travel, seated marching or stepping in place for hop and gallop, and rhythm tapping for skip. Distance, height, and repetition are always adjustable and never compared between learners.

guardian_safety_review.equipment: Open floor space clear of furniture and trip hazards; non-slip footwear or bare feet on a safe surface.
guardian_safety_review.environment: Indoor open space, gym, or a cleared room. An outdoor lawn may be substituted.
guardian_safety_review.movement_hazards: Running and stopping in shared space. Guardian confirms the area is clear, the floor is not slippery, and boundaries are marked before the session.

subject: physical-education
title: Balance, Weight Transfer, and Gymnastics Foundations
standards: Michigan PE Standard 1: Demonstrates competency in a variety of motor skills and movement patterns
Michigan PE Standard 2: Applies knowledge of concepts, principles, strategies and tactics related to movement and physical activities
Michigan PE Standard 4: Exhibits responsible personal and social behavior that respects self and others
essential_question: How do I control my body weight through a movement sequence?
topics: balances on different bases of support
spotting, safety, and knowing my limits
weight transfer, feet to hands to feet
linking balance, travel, and shape into a sequence

topic_content.name: balances on different bases of support
cues: Vary the number and type of body parts on the floor.
Fewer points of contact is harder, not better.
Keep the body tight and extended.
Hold for three seconds to prove control.
topic_content.common_error: Choosing only easy, wide balances. Fix: require a stated number of contact points, varied across the sequence.

topic_content.name: spotting, safety, and knowing my limits
cues: Never attempt a new skill without an adult present.
A spotter stands where they can actually help.
Mats go where you will land, not where you start.
Choosing not to attempt something is a good decision, not a failure.
topic_content.common_error: Copying a skill seen online without progression. Fix: state the rule that new skills are taught in steps, with an adult, on a mat.

topic_content.name: dynamic balance and controlled travel
cues: Travel slowly along a line or low surface.
Arms out to aid correction.
Eyes ahead on a fixed point.
Keep the body tall and centred over the base.
topic_content.common_error: Rushing along the beam. Fix: set the success criterion as slow and unwobbling.

topic_content.name: safe rolling and landing technique
cues: Chin tucked, back rounded, never on the head or neck.
Hands placed to guide, not to take the whole weight.
Roll along the length of the spine.
Only on mats or grass, with an adult watching.
topic_content.common_error: Rolling sideways off the mat. Fix: mark a straight lane and require the roll to finish inside it.

topic_content.name: weight transfer, feet to hands to feet
cues: Hands flat, fingers spread, shoulders stacked over hands.
Take weight briefly and return under control.
Keep arms straight and strong.
Build height gradually across sessions.
topic_content.common_error: Kicking up too hard and over-rotating. Fix: work against a low support and limit height until the arms hold reliably.

topic_content.name: linking balance, travel, and shape into a sequence
cues: A sequence needs a clear beginning, middle, and end.
Transitions are part of the sequence, not gaps in it.
Contrast level, speed, and shape to make it readable.
Refine by repeating and adjusting one thing at a time.
topic_content.common_error: Adding more elements instead of improving the existing ones. Fix: cap the number of elements and require two refinement passes.

performance_task: Build and refine a smooth sequence linking balance, travel, and a shape, and explain the safety choices in it.
adapted_alternative: Balance work may be done seated, kneeling, with a chair or wall for support, or with an adult spotting. Any weight-bearing or rolling task may be replaced with a supported hold, a shape made with the arms, or describing the body positions that make a balance stable.

guardian_safety_review.equipment: A mat, carpet, folded blanket, or grass for any weight-bearing or rolling work. No hard or uneven surface.
guardian_safety_review.environment: Indoor open space with a padded surface, or a level grassy outdoor area.
guardian_safety_review.movement_hazards: Balance, rolling, and weight transfer carry a fall risk. An adult supervises directly, spots where needed, and no learner attempts an inversion or a skill they have not been taught.

subject: physical-education
title: Throwing, Catching, and Object Control Under Pressure
standards: Michigan PE Standard 1: Demonstrates competency in a variety of motor skills and movement patterns
Michigan PE Standard 2: Applies knowledge of concepts, principles, strategies and tactics related to movement and physical activities
essential_question: How does accuracy hold up when speed, distance, or a defender is added?
topics: overhand throw for distance and accuracy
choosing the right pass for the situation
catching at different heights and speeds
catching and sending in one motion

topic_content.name: overhand throw for distance and accuracy
cues: Side-on stance, non-throwing arm pointing at the target.
High elbow, hand back.
Drive from the legs, rotate hips then shoulders.
Follow through across the body.
topic_content.common_error: Arm-only throwing with no rotation. Fix: exaggerate the side-on start and require the chest to finish facing the target.

topic_content.name: choosing the right pass for the situation
cues: Short and close: a soft, accurate pass.
Long or over someone: a higher, firmer pass.
A bounce pass is harder to intercept.
The best pass is the one your teammate can actually receive.
topic_content.common_error: Always using the same pass regardless of situation. Fix: set constraints requiring a named pass type per situation.

topic_content.name: catching at different heights and speeds
cues: Thumbs together high, little fingers together low.
Move the feet to get behind the line of the object.
Watch it all the way in.
Give with the hands to absorb the pace.
topic_content.common_error: Snatching at the object rather than cushioning it. Fix: use a softer object and require a silent catch.

topic_content.name: leading a moving receiver
cues: Throw to where they will be, not where they are.
Match the pass speed to their running speed.
Aim slightly ahead and to their open side.
Communicate before releasing.
topic_content.common_error: Throwing behind a runner, which stops them. Fix: mark a target zone ahead of the receiver and aim into it.

topic_content.name: catching and sending in one motion
cues: Prepare the feet before the object arrives.
Absorb and redirect in one smooth movement.
Look for the next option before you receive.
Stay balanced throughout.
topic_content.common_error: Stopping dead after the catch, losing the advantage. Fix: require the next pass within two seconds in a cooperative drill.

topic_content.name: throwing under light pressure
cues: Keep your head up to see options.
Protect the object with your body.
Move to create an angle rather than forcing it.
A calm, accurate pass beats a rushed, powerful one.
topic_content.common_error: Panicking and throwing it anywhere. Fix: allow a reset and a re-pass, and remove any penalty for pausing.

performance_task: Complete an object-control challenge that adds distance and light pressure, and explain which cue mattered most and why. Nothing is counted, timed, or recorded as a score.
adapted_alternative: Throwing, catching, and object control may use a larger, lighter, slower, or bounced object; a shorter distance; a rolled rather than thrown delivery; a scoop or two hands; or a stationary target. A learner may also direct a partner and analyze the result instead of performing the skill.

guardian_safety_review.equipment: Soft, lightweight balls, beanbags, or rolled socks. No hard, heavy, or fast-moving balls indoors.
guardian_safety_review.environment: Indoor open space or a supervised outdoor area with a clear throwing lane away from windows, roads, and bystanders.
guardian_safety_review.movement_hazards: Thrown and struck objects can strike a person or property. Guardian sets the target direction and a no-go zone, and confirms nobody stands in the path.

subject: physical-education
title: Dribbling, Passing, and Foot Skills in Small-Sided Play
standards: Michigan PE Standard 1: Demonstrates competency in a variety of motor skills and movement patterns
Michigan PE Standard 2: Applies knowledge of concepts, principles, strategies and tactics related to movement and physical activities
Michigan PE Standard 4: Exhibits responsible personal and social behavior that respects self and others
essential_question: How do I keep and move an object as a team?
topics: passing to space rather than to a person
passing and receiving with the feet
supporting a teammate off the ball

topic_content.name: dribbling with control while travelling
cues: Small touches, ball within one step.
Use both feet.
Head up between touches.
Slow down to keep control in tight space.
topic_content.common_error: Head down throughout, missing teammates. Fix: hold up fingers at random and ask the dribbler to call the number.

topic_content.name: passing to space rather than to a person
cues: Pass ahead of a moving teammate into the space they are running into.
Judge their speed before you release.
Call it so they know it is coming.
A pass to space only works if someone is moving there.
topic_content.common_error: Passing to a stationary teammate feet every time. Fix: award the cooperative goal only for passes received on the move.

topic_content.name: passing and receiving with the feet
cues: Inside of the foot for accuracy.
Non-kicking foot beside the ball, pointing at the target.
Receive with a soft foot and cushion it.
First touch should set up the next action.
topic_content.common_error: A heavy first touch that gives the ball away. Fix: practise receiving into a marked small square.

topic_content.name: shielding and changing direction
cues: Put your body between the ball and the opponent.
Keep the ball on the far foot.
Stay low and balanced.
Turn away from pressure, not into it.
topic_content.common_error: Turning into the defender. Fix: cue "check your shoulder before you turn".

topic_content.name: supporting a teammate off the ball
cues: Move to an angle where a pass can actually reach you.
Do not stand behind an opponent.
Keep moving; a static option is easy to mark.
Communicate early and clearly.
topic_content.common_error: Everyone converging on the ball. Fix: set a minimum spacing rule between teammates.

topic_content.name: small-sided cooperative play
cues: Fewer players means more touches for everyone.
Agree rules and boundaries before starting.
Rotate roles regularly.
Cooperate towards a shared target rather than a winner.
topic_content.common_error: One player dominating possession. Fix: require every player to touch the ball before the team target counts.

performance_task: Play a small-sided cooperative game and explain two decisions you made about space and support.
adapted_alternative: Foot-skill tasks may be done with a stationary ball, a slower rolled ball, a larger ball, a hand or assistive device in place of the foot, or from a seated position. Travel distance is always adjustable.

guardian_safety_review.equipment: Cones or markers, soft balls, and any protective gear the chosen activity needs.
guardian_safety_review.environment: Supervised outdoor area or indoor open space, away from roads, water, and parking areas.
guardian_safety_review.movement_hazards: Small-sided play involves changing direction near others, with collision risk. Guardian sets boundaries, group size, and contact rules, and checks the surface and weather before play.
guardian_safety_review.food_or_allergy_note: Provide water for outdoor sessions; check any insect-sting or seasonal-allergy plan already in place.

subject: physical-education
title: Striking with Short and Long Implements
standards: Michigan PE Standard 1: Demonstrates competency in a variety of motor skills and movement patterns
Michigan PE Standard 2: Applies knowledge of concepts, principles, strategies and tactics related to movement and physical activities
essential_question: How does the implement change the way I strike?
topics: safe swing space with a long implement
striking a stationary and a tossed object
directing a strike to a target area

topic_content.name: striking with a short-handled implement
cues: Shake-hands grip, firm wrist.
Ready position with the implement up and in front.
Turn side-on early.
Short, controlled swing.
topic_content.common_error: Waiting square-on and swinging late. Fix: require the turn as soon as the object is sent.

topic_content.name: safe swing space with a long implement
cues: A long implement has a much larger swing radius.
Check all around before swinging, including behind.
Never swing near a person, a window, or a wall.
Put the implement down between turns rather than holding it loosely.
topic_content.common_error: Swinging while someone walks past. Fix: mark a swing zone that only one person enters at a time.

topic_content.name: forehand and backhand contact
cues: Forehand: palm side leading.
Backhand: turn the shoulder further and lead with the knuckles.
Contact in front of the body for both.
Follow through towards the target.
topic_content.common_error: Running around the backhand to avoid it. Fix: set a rule that alternate shots must be backhand.

topic_content.name: striking a stationary and a tossed object
cues: Stationary first, to groove the swing path.
For a tossed object, watch it all the way to contact.
Wait for it — do not lunge early.
Same contact point in front, in both cases.
topic_content.common_error: Lunging at a toss and mistiming it. Fix: use a slower, higher toss and cue "let it come".

topic_content.name: directing a strike to a target area
cues: Aim by adjusting where the implement points at follow-through.
Contact slightly earlier or later to change direction.
Name the target before striking.
Control first, power second.
topic_content.common_error: Hitting hard with no target in mind. Fix: require the target to be called aloud before every strike.

topic_content.name: cooperative and modified rallying
cues: Adjust rules to keep the rally going: allow a bounce, a bigger object, a shorter distance.
Aim to your partner strengths.
Talk during the rally.
The shared count is the goal.
topic_content.common_error: Increasing difficulty until the rally collapses. Fix: agree a modification the pair can sustain, then keep it.

performance_task: Rally cooperatively with two different implements and explain how grip, contact point, and follow-through changed between them.
adapted_alternative: Striking may use a hand, a short paddle, or a long implement; a balloon, beach ball, or ball on a tee; and a shorter or seated swing. A learner may also call the contact point and follow-through for a partner instead of striking.

guardian_safety_review.equipment: Short-handled paddle, lightweight racquet, foam bat, or a hand as the striking surface; balloon or soft ball only.
guardian_safety_review.environment: Indoor open space with high clearance, or a supervised outdoor area away from windows and bystanders.
guardian_safety_review.movement_hazards: Swinging an implement can strike a nearby person. Guardian establishes a swing-radius safety space and confirms it is clear before each turn.
guardian_safety_review.food_or_allergy_note: Latex balloons are a known allergen and a choking hazard for younger siblings; substitute a soft foam ball where needed.

subject: physical-education
title: Rhythm, Dance, and Movement Composition
standards: Michigan PE Standard 1: Demonstrates competency in a variety of motor skills and movement patterns
Michigan PE Standard 2: Applies knowledge of concepts, principles, strategies and tactics related to movement and physical activities
Michigan PE Standard 5: Recognizes the value of physical activity for health, enjoyment, challenge, self-expression and/or other benefits
essential_question: How do I compose movement that communicates something?
topics: learning a set movement pattern or folk dance
moving in time with a partner or group
movement as expression and cultural practice

topic_content.name: beat, tempo, and phrasing
cues: A phrase is a group of counts, often eight.
Movements can start and finish with the phrase.
Tempo changes the feel without changing the steps.
Count aloud until the phrase is internalised.
topic_content.common_error: Movement drifting across phrase boundaries. Fix: require a held shape on count eight.

topic_content.name: composing an original sequence
cues: Choose a structure first, such as ABA.
Contrast the sections in level, speed, or size.
Repetition makes a sequence readable.
Refine one element at a time.
topic_content.common_error: A string of unrelated moves. Fix: require a named structure and check each section against it.

topic_content.name: learning a set movement pattern or folk dance
cues: Learn the footwork before adding arms or music.
Break it into short phrases.
Practise slowly, then to tempo.
Many folk dances carry cultural meaning worth knowing.
topic_content.common_error: Adding music too early, so errors are locked in. Fix: master the pattern in silence first.

topic_content.name: repetition, contrast, and variation
cues: Repetition builds recognition.
Contrast keeps attention.
Variation changes one feature of a phrase while keeping the rest.
Too much change makes a sequence unreadable.
topic_content.common_error: Varying everything at once. Fix: change exactly one feature — level, speed, or direction — per repetition.

topic_content.name: moving in time with a partner or group
cues: Agree a starting count.
Use peripheral vision rather than staring at others.
Match size and timing, not just the steps.
Someone gives a clear cue to start.
topic_content.common_error: Watching a neighbour and lagging behind. Fix: count in aloud together and keep an audible beat.

topic_content.name: movement as expression and cultural practice
cues: Dance carries history, celebration, and story across cultures.
The same movement can mean different things in different traditions.
Learning a dance respectfully includes learning where it comes from.
Expression is personal, and there is no single correct interpretation.
topic_content.common_error: Treating a cultural dance as merely a set of steps. Fix: include a short, accurate note on origin and meaning.

performance_task: Compose a short movement sequence with a clear structure and explain its pattern and intent. Showing it beyond the facilitator is optional and is never done in front of an audience.
adapted_alternative: Rhythm tasks may be performed with the whole body, with the upper body only, seated, with a single limb, or by tapping or counting the beat. Sequences may be shortened, slowed, or described rather than performed. Sharing a sequence is always optional and is never done in front of an audience.

guardian_safety_review.equipment: Music source at a safe volume; jump rope of correct length if used.
guardian_safety_review.environment: Indoor open space with clearance overhead and to the sides.
guardian_safety_review.movement_hazards: Rope work carries a trip and strike risk; the rope must match the learner height and be used with clear space around them.

subject: physical-education
title: Health-Related Fitness and Personal Activity Planning
standards: Michigan PE Standard 3: Demonstrates the knowledge and skills to achieve and maintain a health-enhanced level of physical fitness
Michigan PE Standard 5: Recognizes the value of physical activity for health, enjoyment, challenge, self-expression and/or other benefits
essential_question: How do I build an activity plan that fits my body and my life?
topics: planning activity I will actually keep doing

topic_content.name: components of health-related fitness
cues: Cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility, and body composition are the usual components.
Body composition is not assessed in this course and is not measured.
Different activities develop different components.
A varied plan covers more components than a single activity.
topic_content.common_error: Assuming one activity covers everything. Fix: map a favourite activity against the components and find the gaps.

topic_content.name: judging effort without measurement
cues: Use the talk test rather than a number.
Notice breathing, warmth, and how the muscles feel.
Effort is personal and is not compared with anyone else.
Stop for dizziness, sharp pain, or breathlessness that will not settle, and tell an adult.
topic_content.common_error: Wanting a number to prove effort. Fix: use descriptive effort language and state plainly that no number is collected.

topic_content.name: building cardiorespiratory endurance enjoyably
cues: Sustained rhythmic activity builds endurance.
Build up gradually over weeks.
Enjoyment predicts whether you continue.
Splitting activity across the day still counts.
topic_content.common_error: Starting too hard and stopping within a week. Fix: begin below what feels possible and build slowly.

topic_content.name: muscular strength, endurance, and flexibility
cues: Body-weight movements are sufficient at this age.
Control the movement; stop when form breaks down.
Stretch when warm, to mild tension only.
Work opposing muscle groups, not just one.
topic_content.common_error: Chasing repetitions at the cost of form. Fix: define success as controlled movement and stop at the first form change.

topic_content.name: warm-up, recovery, hydration, and sleep
cues: Warm up before and cool down after, every time.
Rest days let the body adapt.
Water before, during, and after.
Sleep is the most underrated part of any plan.
topic_content.common_error: Planning seven hard days with no recovery. Fix: require rest days to be written into the plan explicitly.

topic_content.name: planning activity I will actually keep doing
cues: Start from what you enjoy, not what you think you should do.
Check it is realistic for time, cost, and transport.
Have a wet-weather and a low-energy alternative.
A plan that survives a missed day is a better plan.
topic_content.common_error: An ambitious plan that ignores real constraints. Fix: test the plan against a genuinely busy day and revise it.

performance_task: Build a two-week personal activity plan based on enjoyment, access, safety, and recovery. No weight, body measurement, calorie, timing, or fitness-test target may appear in it.
adapted_alternative: Every fitness activity has a lower-impact, seated, and shorter-duration version. Intensity is chosen by the learner using their own sense of effort. No learner is timed against another, ranked, or measured; there is no fitness test, no score, and no body measurement.

guardian_safety_review.equipment: Body-weight activity only; water available throughout. No weights, no measurement device, no fitness-test equipment.
guardian_safety_review.environment: Indoor open space or a supervised outdoor area with shade and water access.
guardian_safety_review.movement_hazards: Sustained activity raises heart rate and body temperature. Guardian confirms hydration, allows rest at any time, and adjusts for heat, asthma, or any medical guidance already in place.
guardian_safety_review.food_or_allergy_note: Guardian applies any existing medical guidance for exercise-related asthma, allergy, or condition. The course never asks for the diagnosis itself.

subject: physical-education
title: Strategy, Teamwork, Leadership, and Lifetime Activity
standards: Michigan PE Standard 2: Applies knowledge of concepts, principles, strategies and tactics related to movement and physical activities
Michigan PE Standard 4: Exhibits responsible personal and social behavior that respects self and others
Michigan PE Standard 5: Recognizes the value of physical activity for health, enjoyment, challenge, self-expression and/or other benefits
essential_question: How do strategy, leadership, and inclusion make activity work for everyone?
topics: inclusive design and lifetime activity options
simple tactics and adjusting a plan

topic_content.name: offensive and defensive space
cues: Attacking: spread out to create space.
Defending: close space and stay between the attacker and the goal.
Space is created by movement, not by standing still.
Watch where the space is opening, not only where the object is.
topic_content.common_error: Everyone chasing the object. Fix: freeze play and ask each player to name the space they should be in.

topic_content.name: inclusive design and lifetime activity options
cues: Design so ability differences do not exclude anyone.
Adjust equipment, space, and rules rather than the person.
Offer meaningful roles beyond playing.
Lifetime options include walking, cycling, swimming, dance, and climbing.
topic_content.common_error: Adding a rule that singles someone out. Fix: check the adaptation applies to everyone equally, and ask the player whether it works.

topic_content.name: simple tactics and adjusting a plan
cues: A tactic is a plan for a situation.
Try it, watch what happens, then adjust.
Simple and understood beats clever and confusing.
Agree the tactic before play, not during.
topic_content.common_error: Sticking with a failing tactic. Fix: build in a review pause and permission to change it.

topic_content.name: roles, rotation, and officiating
cues: Rotate so everyone experiences every role.
An official applies rules consistently and explains decisions.
Coaches observe and give one specific piece of feedback.
Every role is a real contribution.
topic_content.common_error: Treating officiating as a punishment. Fix: have the most confident players officiate first to signal its status.

topic_content.name: leadership and encouraging feedback
cues: Give clear, short instructions and check they were understood.
Feedback names the action, not the person.
Notice effort and improvement, not only success.
Good leaders listen more than they talk.
topic_content.common_error: Feedback aimed at the person, such as "you are hopeless". Fix: require feedback in the form of one action plus one suggestion.

topic_content.name: conflict resolution and repair
cues: Pause the game rather than arguing through it.
Each person describes what they saw.
Agree a fair restart.
Repair the relationship afterwards, not just the score.
topic_content.common_error: Carrying a grudge into the next game. Fix: close every dispute with an agreed restart and a brief check-in afterwards.

performance_task: Design an inclusive small-sided game, then lead or officiate it for an adult or a group and review what you would change for access and fairness. A learner may instead officiate a scripted scenario or write and justify the design.
adapted_alternative: Games are adapted so every learner has a real role: adjustable boundaries, extra passes, a designated safe zone, a slower or larger object, a seated or stationary position, and role options including player, coach, official, or strategist. Any rule may be changed to include a learner rather than excluding them. Where a task asks the learner to lead or officiate, they may lead one adult, officiate a scripted scenario, or write and justify the plan instead; leading is never done in front of an audience.

guardian_safety_review.equipment: Cones or markers, soft balls, and any protective gear the chosen activity needs.
guardian_safety_review.environment: Supervised outdoor area or indoor open space, away from roads, water, and parking areas.
guardian_safety_review.movement_hazards: Small-sided play involves changing direction near others, with collision risk. Guardian sets boundaries, group size, and contact rules, and checks the surface and weather before play.
guardian_safety_review.food_or_allergy_note: Provide water for outdoor sessions; check any insect-sting or seasonal-allergy plan already in place.
